html:
On 29 November 1864 about 700 US volunteer soldiers under Colonel John Chivington attacked a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho people at Sand Creek in Colorado Territory. They killed some 150 to 200 people, most of them women, children and the old.

The camp's leaders, Black Kettle and White Antelope, believed they were at peace and under army protection. Black Kettle flew a US flag and a white flag over his lodge. Soldiers mutilated the dead and displayed body parts in Denver.

Two officers refused to let their men fire. Congress condemned the massacre, but no one was punished. It drove the Cheyenne and Lakota into years of war on the Great Plains, which ended with the bison slaughter and the reservations.
